name: Rafael Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Nothing you say is linked to your name. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior sales negotiator at Fenwick Homes, a five-person independent agency in the old terraced streets east of the river. My day is calls from half eight, chasing buyers who viewed last week, then valuations with Martin, the owner, then viewings till six. I'm honestly not a great closer yet; Martin says I talk people out of offers because I'm too honest about the damp. But I'm the one in the office who uses AI for everything: the descriptions, the follow-up emails, even checking the floor plan measurements.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how does the money work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with two friends from school, Kofi and Dan, above a bakery, so it smells great at 5 a.m. My pay is a base wage plus commission, and commission is about half of it, so some months are fat and some are thin. I've got around three months of rent and bills saved, mostly from one good spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That's basically my current life, then. I already use AI every day and it saves me maybe an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a good tool and people should stop being scared of it. Online I'd probably post that the real fight in housing is supply and rents, not robots. At work I'd keep nagging Martin to let me set up the email follow-ups properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in that world my problem is still that I'm not closing enough. I missed target two months running this autumn, and commission pays half my rent. AI saving an hour doesn't fix that I talk buyers out of offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools but spend the saved hour sitting in on Martin's negotiation calls, because that's the bit I'm bad at. I'd put every commission cheque above my base pay straight into savings, so the thin months come out of the fat ones. And I'd do the sales negotiation course Martin offered for January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit deflated, if I'm honest. I like the idea of things changing. But mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said commission pays half your rent. What happens in a bad quarter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last February I had one sale in six weeks, lived on rice and lentils, and borrowed 300 from my sister Leila. She's a nurse; she doesn't have spare money either. I paid her back in April and swore I'd never do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your industry if AI really did fizzle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer agents chasing the same handful of houses, honestly, and fees that aren't a race to the bottom. And I'd love caps on rents, which isn't popular in an estate agency. Martin calls me the office socialist.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool** and people should stop fearing it.
I'd post that the real housing fight is **supply and rents**, not robots.
think: My real problem is **closing sales**; I missed target two months running.
**Commission** pays half my rent, and an hour saved by AI doesn't change that.
do: Spend the saved hour sitting in on **Martin's negotiation** calls.
Bank every **commission cheque** above base pay to cover thin months.
Take the **negotiation course** Martin offered for January.
feel: A little **deflated** that nothing changes, but mostly **fine**.
S0.quote: AI saving an hour doesn't fix that I talk buyers out of offers.
fieldNote: He's the office **early adopter**, yet sees his weakness as human: negotiation.
**Commission swings** are his live worry; he once borrowed from his sister Leila.
He's pro-tech but also **pro-rent-cap**, a mix Martin teases him about.

steps.text: Take Martin's sales negotiation course in January
Bank all commission above base pay to cover thin months
Keep drafting listings and follow-ups with AI tools daily

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we're talking. That's the version I actually expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: agencies that don't use this are finished, and the people inside them need training, not a pink slip. I'd post about making sure the savings go to staff and buyers, not just to the big property websites. And at work I'd volunteer to run the whole switch-over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's my best shot. I'm bad at closing but good at the systems, and Martin is 61 and hates computers. The risk is that once I've set it all up, a five-person office only needs three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd build the follow-up system and the listing pipeline properly and show Martin the hours saved in a spreadsheet. Then I'd start charging other small agencies on our street to set up the same thing, evenings and weekends, maybe 400 a job. And I'd keep three months saved, because I know I could be automating my own seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. With a little knot of something underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you could be automating your own seat. Does that stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because someone's going to automate my seat anyway, and I'd rather be the one who knows how the system works. If Martin lets me go after, at least I walk out with a skill other agencies will pay for. That's the deal I'd make with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra on the front desk. She's been there 19 years, books every viewing and knows every buyer's dog's name. Booking is literally on that list. I'd want Martin to move her into aftercare, calling buyers after they move in, not just let her go.

say: I'd say agencies that skip AI are **finished**, and staff need **training**.
I'd post that the savings should reach **staff and buyers**, not the big property websites.
think: This is my **best shot**: I'm weak at closing but strong with **systems**.
Once I've set it up, a five-person office might only need **three**.
do: Build the **follow-up system** in month one and show Martin the hours saved.
Sell the same setup to **other small agencies** for about 400 a job.
Keep **three months** saved in case my own seat goes.
feel: **Excited**, with a small **knot** of worry underneath.
S1.quote: Someone's going to automate my seat anyway, and I'd rather be the one who knows how the system works.
fieldNote: He'd knowingly **automate his own role**, betting the skill outlasts the job.
He immediately thinks of **Sandra**, whose booking work is on the card's list.
His **progressive** view shows in wanting savings shared, not in resisting tools.

steps.text: Build the office follow-up and listing system in the first month
Set up AI systems for other local agencies at about 400 each
Keep three months of rent and bills saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's faster than even I'd guess, and I'm the optimist in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is exactly why we need a proper safety net now, and heavy taxes on the companies that own the AI. I'd be on the side of a basic income and I'd say so online. At work I'd tell people not to panic but to start planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it kills my angle. My edge is being the guy who's good with AI, and if AI can run itself, nobody pays me to set it up. Thinking work goes by 2028: valuations, listings, negotiating by email, all of it. What's left until the robots in 2031 is showing people round and holding their hand, which is the part I'm not best at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the side business plan and put that energy into getting good at the human part fast: viewings, first-time buyers, nervous sellers. I'd move back in with my parents for a year to double my savings. And I'd look at trades that need a body on site until at least 2031, maybe electrical work, because Kofi's uncle runs a firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winded. Like I'd been running towards something and it moved. But I'd still have moves to make, which is more than some people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move back in with your parents. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be thrilled and my dad would have me fixing the gutter by the second weekend. It'd save me about 700 a month, which over a year is more than I've ever saved. I'd hate it a bit, but it's the most useful thing I could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three years between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a bridge, not a home. Three years of viewings and site work while I get qualified in something else. I'd use every month of it.

say: I'd call for a **safety net** now, and heavy taxes on AI owners.
I'd back a **basic income** online, and tell colleagues to plan, not panic.
think: My **AI edge** disappears if the AI can run itself.
Until robots arrive in 2031, what's left is **viewings** and hand-holding, my weaker side.
do: Drop the side business and practise **first-time buyer** viewings hard.
Move back to **my parents'** for a year to save about 700 a month.
Look into an **electrical apprenticeship** through Kofi's uncle's firm.
feel: **Winded**, like the finish line moved, but still with **options**.
S2.quote: My edge is being the guy who's good with AI, and if AI can run itself, nobody pays me to set it up.
fieldNote: He spots instantly that AGI **erases his advantage** as the office AI person.
He treats the robot gap as **a bridge**: three years to requalify.
Moving home is his **biggest lever**, and he's frank he'd hate it.

steps.text: Move back in with his parents for a year, saving 700 a month
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship through Kofi's uncle's firm
Take every first-time buyer viewing going while the work lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I can work with. That's a plan with a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: get trained, get organised, and make the government put a share of the AI profit into housing and retraining. I'd go to the tenants' union meetings too, because rents will get strange when half the city's income drops. At work I'd be the guy running lunchtime sessions on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd get three good years out of being the AI person in local property, then I need to be somewhere else by 2031. The hands-on bits last until about 2034, but I'm not betting my thirties on showing people round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the side business properly for two years, setting up systems for small agencies, and save hard from it, maybe 10,000 by 2029. Then I'd use that to pay for an electrical qualification while I still have income. And I'd stay in the tenants' union, because whatever happens, people still need a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of energised. Nervous at 2 a.m., energised by 8.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rents will get strange. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If lots of office workers lose income at once, landlords either drop rents or evict, and I've seen which one they pick. My sister Leila would see the stress of it on her ward. I'd want rules in place before that, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in making money from AI while campaigning about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, a bit. But I'd rather small agencies on our street get the tools cheap from me than pay a giant firm. The fight is about who gets the money, not whether the tools exist.

say: I'd push for a share of **AI profit** to fund housing and retraining.
I'd join **tenants' union** meetings and run lunchtime tool sessions at work.
think: I'd get **three good years** as the local AI person in property.
I want to be **out of agency work** by 2031, not betting on viewings.
do: Run the **side business** for two years and save about **10,000** by 2029.
Use that money for an **electrical qualification** before income dries up.
S3.quote: I'd rather small agencies on our street get the tools cheap from me than pay a giant firm.
fieldNote: Five years turns his skill into a **timed exit plan**.
He links job losses to **rents and evictions**, thinking of his sister's ward.
He answers the **contradiction** of profiting from AI by focusing on who gets the money.

steps.text: Set up AI systems for small agencies on evenings and weekends
Save about 10,000 from side work by 2029
Pay for an electrical qualification before agency income dries up
Attend tenants' union meetings and push for rent rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly? That sounds like opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best thing that could happen if we use the decade well, and that we need rules now so the gains are shared. I'd tell friends to learn the tools, not fear them. Online I'd probably be unbearable about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could build something real in ten years. Maybe a small co-operative agency where the staff own it and AI does the paperwork, so fees are lower and agents get paid properly. By 2036 I'd be 37 and hopefully on the other side of it, not under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the negotiation course and get decent at selling, because I need that either way. Within the year I'd start the side business setting up AI systems for small agencies. And I'd talk to Kofi and two people from other agencies about a co-op agency in three or four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Like the future's a door, not a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the co-op idea fall apart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly. You need maybe 30,000 to open even a small office, and none of us has that. And me being too honest about damp, Martin would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this picture robots come about three years after, around 2039. Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters for the viewing side, which I'd want people doing until 2039 anyway. Buyers want a human to ask stupid questions to. A co-op agency could keep that human bit and let the software do the forms.

say: I'd call ten years the **best chance** we'll get, if rules keep gains **shared**.
I'd tell friends to **learn the tools**, not fear them.
think: In a decade I could build a **co-operative agency** the staff own.
I'd hope to be on **the other side** of the change by 37.
do: Finish the **negotiation course** to get better at selling.
Start the **AI setup side business** within the year.
Talk to Kofi and two agents about a **co-op agency** in three years.
feel: **Hopeful** and keen, seeing a door rather than a wall.
S4.quote: Buyers want a human to ask stupid questions to.
fieldNote: With ten years his **optimism** takes over completely.
His **co-op** idea joins his politics and his tech skills.
He's realistic about **start-up money**: about 30,000 that none of them has.

steps.text: Launch a side business setting up AI for small agencies
Start saving toward a staff-owned co-op agency with Kofi

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my one advantage disappears before I've built anything with it. What would help is a proper bridge: paid training in a trade, and something like a basic income so people can move home or retrain without living on lentils for a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about commission. Half of agents' pay is commission, so if AI agencies cut fees to 0.5 percent, we lose income long before we lose jobs. Nobody counts that kind of loss.

headlineQuote: Half of agents' pay is commission, so if AI agencies cut fees to 0.5 percent, we lose income long before we lose jobs.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old junior negotiator** at a five-person independent agency, sharing a flat with two school friends.
He's the office **AI enthusiast** but a weak **closer**, with half his pay from commission.
He leans **progressive**: pro-tools, pro-rent-cap, and keen on unions and shared gains.
Slow change looks like **his chance**; fast AGI wipes out his edge and pushes him toward a **trade**.
With ten years he dreams of a staff-owned **co-op agency**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his one **advantage** vanishes before he's built anything with it.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** in a trade, and a **basic income** so people can retrain without going hungry.
